claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a naturally formed, non-uniform native oxide film.
Defects and inclusions associated with the native surface can act as initiation sites for localized corrosion.
Acid pickling followed by controlled oxidation can remove the native heterogeneous oxide.
The proposed chemical treatment can grow a uniform, adherent passive Fe-oxide film on Q235 steel.
A uniform passive oxide film reduces surface heterogeneity and the number of active sites for localized galvanic-cell formation.
The continuous, defect-minimized Fe-oxide layer acts as a barrier against the chloride environment.
Residual inclusions or heterogeneous corrosion-product distributions on untreated Q235 steel promote localized galvanic coupling.
Localized galvanic coupling leads to pitting and accelerated corrosion in chloride environments.
Controlled chemical passivation will suppress the onset of localized pitting corrosion relative to untreated Q235 steel.
Passivated specimens will have lower pit density than untreated specimens after 72 hours in 3.5% NaCl at 25°C.
Passivated specimens will have lower pit density than untreated specimens after 72 hours in 3.5% NaCl at approximately 80°C.
Passivated specimens will have a lower overall corrosion rate than untreated specimens at both tested temperatures.
The protective effect may differ under very acidic, extreme-pH, or non-chloride aggressive environments.
